topics.titleEn: Adjective endings after the definite article
topics.summary: Only -e and -en; five boxes take -e, the rest take -en.

explanation.heading: Two endings only
explanation.text: After der, das, die, den, dem the adjective ends in -e or -en — nothing else. The article has already shown the case and gender, so the adjective carries little work.

explanation.heading: Where -e appears
explanation.text: In the nominative of all three genders, and in the accusative of the neuter and the feminine: der lebendige Dialekt, das neue Leben, die lange Tradition.

explanation.heading: Where -en appears
explanation.text: In the accusative masculine, in the whole dative, and in the entire plural: den lebendigen Dialekt, dem neuen Leben, die alten Lieder.

explanation.heading: The dative plural noun too
explanation.text: The table's dative plural is den alten Liedern — the noun itself adds -n.

rules: Nominative M/N/F: -e. Accusative N/F: -e.
Accusative M: -en.
Dative in every gender and number: -en.
Plural in every case: -en.
In the dative plural the noun adds -n as well: den alten Liedern.

examples.note: Akkusativ M — the only accusative with -en
Dativ Plural — noun ends in -n as well

exercises.explain: Nominative masculine after der takes -e.
Accusative masculine takes -en.

exercises.prompt: Which form is the dative plural?
exercises.explain: Dative plural: den, -en on the adjective, -n on the noun.
Feminine nominative and accusative take -e.

exercises.prompt: Put the phrase into the dative.
exercises.explain: Feminine dative: der + -en.

exercises.prompt: How many different endings does this table use?
exercises.explain: After the definite article only -e and -en occur.

topics.summary: With no article the adjective takes over the article's own ending.

explanation.heading: The adjective stands in for the article
explanation.text: The table is written as a set of arrows — der → lebendiger Dialekt, das → neues Leben — because the ending the missing article would have had moves onto the adjective.

explanation.heading: How to work it out
explanation.text: Think of the definite article the phrase would take, strip the d-, and put what is left on the adjective: dem → -em, der → -er, den → -en.

explanation.heading: Where you meet it
explanation.text: Mass nouns and plurals without an article: neues Leben, lange Tradition, alte Lieder.

rules: Nominative: -er (M), -es (N), -e (F), -e (plural).
Accusative: -en (M); the neuter, feminine and plural endings are unchanged.
Dative: -em (M and N), -er (F), -en (plural).
In the dative plural the noun still adds -n: alten Liedern.

exercises.explain: der → -er on the adjective.
das → -es on the adjective.

exercises.explain: dem → -em.

topics.titleEn: Adjective endings after ein-, kein-, mein-
topics.summary: Where ein has no ending, the adjective supplies it.

explanation.heading: The mixed pattern
explanation.text: ein, kein and mein behave like the definite article except in three boxes, where they have no ending of their own: nominative masculine, nominative neuter and accusative neuter.

explanation.heading: What the adjective does there
explanation.text: In exactly those three boxes the adjective takes the strong ending instead: ein neuer Trend, ein festliches Kleid, ein schwarzes Barett.

explanation.heading: Everywhere else -en
explanation.text: Accusative masculine, the whole dative and the whole plural take -en: meinen teuren Anzug, meinem schwarzen Talar, meinen stolzen Eltern.

explanation.heading: The plural column
explanation.text: The table pairs the plural with an article-less form: schwarze Talare beside meine / keine männlichen Kollegen — ein- itself has no plural.

rules: Nominative M: -er (ein neuer Trend), because ein has no ending.
Nominative and accusative N: -es (ein festliches Kleid, ein schwarzes Barett).
Nominative and accusative F: -e (eine neue Phase, eine große Party).
Accusative M, the whole dative and the whole plural: -en.
kein- and the possessive articles follow ein- exactly.

examples.note: Nominativ M — the adjective carries the -er

exercises.explain: ein has no ending in the nominative masculine, so the adjective takes -er.
Neuter nominative and accusative: -es.
Accusative masculine: meinen + -en.
The whole dative takes -en.

exercises.explain: Feminine dative: einer + -en.

topics.summary: -en after any article; -er only when there is no article.

explanation.heading: The simplest case of all
explanation.text: The table sets four columns side by side — definite article, indefinite article, possessive article, no article — and in the first three the adjective always ends in -en.

explanation.heading: The exception
explanation.text: Without an article the adjective takes -er in the feminine and in the plural: kurzer Karriere, gestresster Manager. The masculine and neuter keep -en, because the noun itself already shows the genitive with -s.

explanation.heading: The gap in the table
explanation.text: The plural row prints a dash under the indefinite article: ein- has no plural, so there is nothing to show.

rules: After der/die/das, ein-, kein- and the possessive articles: -en in every gender and number.
With no article, M and N: -en (großen Erfolgs, großen Lebens) — the noun's -s carries the case.
With no article, F and plural: -er (kurzer Karriere, gestresster Manager).
ein- has no genitive plural.

examples.note: no article, F — the one place -er appears

exercises.explain: After any article the genitive adjective takes -en.
Feminine genitive with no article takes -er.
Only the article-less plural takes -er.

options: the noun's -s already marks the genitive
answers: the noun's -s already marks the genitive
exercises.explain: M and N genitive nouns add -s, so the adjective stays weak.

exercises.explain: The ending does not change — only the article is added.

explanation.heading: A genitive hanging off another noun
explanation.text: Each phrase has a head noun with its own article — der Genuss, ein Beispiel, Fisch, ein Fotomotiv — followed by an article-less genitive that says what of.

explanation.heading: M and N take -en
explanation.text: der Genuss frischen Fisches, ein Beispiel erfolgreichen Engagements — the genitive -es on the noun does the identifying work.

explanation.heading: F and plural take -er

explanation.heading: Register
explanation.text: This is written, fairly formal German — advertising, journalism, reports.

rules: Masculine and neuter: adjective in -en, noun in -es / -s.
Feminine and plural: adjective in -er, noun unchanged.
The genitive phrase follows the noun it belongs to.

topics.summary: -er and am …sten, plus the umlauts and the five irregulars.

explanation.heading: The regular pattern
explanation.text: Add -er for the comparative and am …sten for the superlative: attraktiv, attraktiver, am attraktivsten.

explanation.heading: When -esten appears
explanation.text: Adjectives ending in -t, -d, -s, -ß or -z insert an e in the superlative: bekannt → am bekanntesten, alt → am ältesten.

explanation.heading: Umlaut
explanation.text: Several short adjectives take an umlaut in both forms: groß → größer → am größten, alt → älter → am ältesten, hoch → höher → am höchsten.

explanation.heading: The irregulars
explanation.text: gut → besser → am besten; gern → lieber → am liebsten; viel → mehr → am meisten; hoch → höher → am höchsten; teuer loses its second e: teurer.

rules: Comparative: adjective + -er. Superlative: am + adjective + -sten.
After -t, -d, -s, -ß, -z the superlative is -esten: am bekanntesten, am ältesten.
groß, alt, hoch take an umlaut: größer, älter, höher.
gut → besser → am besten; gern → lieber → am liebsten; viel → mehr → am meisten.
teuer drops the e of the stem in the comparative: teurer.
hoch loses its c before -er: höher, but am höchsten keeps it.

examples.note: -t forces the extra e in the superlative
the stem loses its e in the comparative

exercises.explain: Regular -er.
Umlaut plus -esten after -t.

exercises.prompt: What is the comparative of gut?
exercises.explain: gut → besser → am besten.

exercises.prompt: What is the comparative of viel?
exercises.explain: viel → mehr → am meisten.
The e of the stem drops out: teurer, not teuerer.
gern → lieber → am liebsten.

topics.summary: wie for equality, als for a difference.

explanation.heading: Equal, or not equal
explanation.text: For etwas / jemand ist gleich / nicht gleich use the basic form with so … wie: genauso gern … wie, nicht so attraktiv wie.

explanation.heading: More
explanation.text: For etwas / jemand ist mehr use the comparative with als: billiger als, gesünder als, mehr Sportmöglichkeiten als.

explanation.heading: lieber … als
explanation.text: The irregular comparative of gern behaves the same way: lieber mit Freunden als allein.

explanation.heading: The commonest mistake
explanation.text: wie never follows a comparative and als never follows so — keep the two frames apart.

rules: Equality: (genau)so + basic form + wie.
Inequality stated as less: nicht so + basic form + wie.
Difference: comparative + als.
mehr + noun + als works the same way as an adjective comparative.
lieber … als is the comparative of gern.

examples.de: Immer mehr Deutsche verbringen ihren Urlaub genauso gern in Deutschland wie im Ausland.
Für den Urlaub findet Niclas die Ostsee nicht so attraktiv wie die Alpen.
Linus meint, Urlaub in Deutschland ist billiger als im Ausland.
Viele denken, die Luft auf dem Land ist gesünder als die Luft in der Stadt.
Niclas möchte lieber mit Freunden als allein in Urlaub fahren.
Niclas findet, die Alpen bieten mehr Sportmöglichkeiten als die Ostsee.

topics.titleEn: Comparative and superlative before a noun
topics.summary: The comparative and superlative keep the ordinary adjective endings.

explanation.heading: Two endings stacked
explanation.text: Before a noun the adjective carries the comparison marker first and the declension ending second: höher + e → höhere, höchst + e → höchste.

explanation.heading: Nothing new to learn
explanation.text: The document states it as a rule: adjectives have the same basic endings when they are in the comparative or superlative form.

explanation.heading: No am here
explanation.text: The predicative superlative am höchsten becomes der höchste Berg before a noun — the article replaces am.

explanation.heading: The one restriction
explanation.text: It is not possible to have a superlative before a noun with the indefinite article, which is why the table's ein- row jumps straight from ein höherer Berg to kein / sein höchster Berg.

rules: The comparison ending comes first, the declension ending second: der höher-e Berg, der höchst-e Berg.
The endings are exactly those of the basic form.
The predicative am …sten is replaced by an article plus the declined superlative.
A superlative cannot stand after ein-; kein- and the possessive articles are fine.
